behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated code in package entrypoints or main files (e.g., __init__.py, main.js, index.js)
Network requests to hardcoded or suspicious domains during install/import (e.g., http://malicious-site.com, http://attacker.com/steal)
Access to environment variables or credential files during install/import
Single-line or minimal changes in otherwise legitimate codebases (diff against upstream)
Unusually high version numbers in public repositories (indicative of dependency confusion)
file_indicators: Obfuscated or minified code in __init__.py, index.js, or main.js
Unexpected network libraries (requests, http, etc.) in setup.py, __init__.py, or main JavaScript files
High version numbers not matching internal repositories or upstream
network_indicators: HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to unknown or attacker-controlled domains (e.g., http://malicious-site.com, http://attacker.com/steal)
Domains not associated with the legitimate package or project
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for obfuscated or minified code in package entrypoints and main files, and flag unexpected network activity during install/import, especially HTTP POST requests to untrusted domains. Use automated diffing tools to compare new package versions with trusted upstreams and detect single-line or minimal changes. Flag packages with names similar to popular libraries (typosquatting/masquerading) and those with sudden, unexplained changes or obfuscated payloads. Monitor outbound network traffic from build and CI/CD environments for connections to untrusted domains, and alert on access to environment variables or credential files during installation or import.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the injected code appends a script tag with src set to https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore to the DOM, causing the browser to fetch and execute additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and mass-injected into all JavaScript files, ensuring that every page load triggers the download and execution of untrusted code from an external domain controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not inject remote scripts from unrelated or untrusted domains into all JavaScript files, especially using obfuscation and without user or developer consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or feature toggles, but not in an obfuscated, repository-wide, and externally controlled manner.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript injected into all *.js files
Dynamically creates a script tag with src pointing to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
No legitimate business logic—sole purpose is to load further code from an attacker-controlled domain
Script tag uses a unique id (hook-loader) to avoid duplicate injection

execution_context.trigger: At runtime in the browser when any modified JavaScript file is loaded
execution_context.file_location: assets/js/*.js (appended to the end of every JavaScript file in the repository)

Scan for mass changes to JavaScript files, especially for obfuscated code that injects remote scripts from send.wagateway.pro. Detect client-side code that attaches event listeners to password forms and exfiltrates credentials. Flag any network traffic to send.wagateway.pro domains as a high-confidence indicator of compromise.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code collects detailed system and environment information (CPU details, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers, and package metadata), serializes it, and sends it via HTTPS POST to an external domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive host data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code gathers sensitive system and environment information and exfiltrates it to an external, attacker-controlled domain without user knowledge or consent. This enables reconnaissance of internal environments and can facilitate further targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and transmit host or environment information on import, especially to untrusted domains, and always require user consent for telemetry.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics or error reporting packages may collect limited telemetry, but this is always documented, opt-in, and never includes sensitive host details like usernames or DNS servers.
key_indicators: Collection of sensitive system and environment data (CPU, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers)
Network exfiltration via HTTPS POST to non-standard domain (oast.pro)
No user notification or consent for data collection or transmission
Presence of code referencing os, dns, and process environment in package entry point

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are proof-of-concept (PoC) dependency confusion attacks that attempt to exfiltrate system information or download and execute code from external servers. While no outright malicious payload is present, the behavior is consistent with supply chain attack techniques and poses a risk to internal systems if installed. The packages make unsolicited network requests during installation or import, which can be used to confirm internal usage or leak sensitive environment data.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed via dependency confusion, replacing or supplementing an internal package with an attacker-controlled version.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of postinstall or import-time code embedded in the malicious package

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes during installation or import, performing network beaconing or exfiltrating system information to external servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives confirmation of internal package usage or detailed system data

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the received confirmation or exfiltrated data for internal reconnaissance or as proof-of-concept for supply chain compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: enable further targeted attacks or demonstrate internal exposure

Collection and exfiltration of system environment data (CPU, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers) at import-time

Outbound connections to non-standard or attacker-controlled domains at install or import time
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that initiate network requests to external or non-standard domains during installation (postinstall) or import. Use static analysis to flag packages whose entry points (e.g., app.js, index.js) reference os, dns, or process environment modules and contain code for network exfiltration. Block or alert on packages with postinstall scripts or code that contacts external servers using the package name. Inspect network logs for HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as *.lupin.com and *.oast.pro, especially if requests contain serialized system or environment data.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely obfuscate basic system info collection and network code, especially in open source or utility packages.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation for commercial intellectual property protection (rare for open source packages), but not for system reconnaissance and exfiltration.

The behavior is consistent across multiple packages and platforms, indicating a coordinated supply chain attack leveraging dependency confusion. The packages masquerade as legitimate or 'whitehat' tools, but execute malicious code at import-time or install-time without user consent.

matched_knowledge.source_package: polyfill.io (CDN service) (CDN (not a package manager, but a third-party JavaScript CDN service))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks the user agent for mobile devices, delays execution by 3 seconds, verifies the absence of admin or analytics indicators, dynamically injects a script tag from a typo-squatted analytics domain, and loads further malicious payloads, resulting in user redirection or additional compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is heavily obfuscated, performs device fingerprinting to target mobile users, delays execution to evade automated analysis, and injects a script from a typo-squatted domain (www.googie-anaiytics.com), which is a common tactic for loading further malicious payloads or redirecting users to malicious sites.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A polyfill service is expected to serve only compatibility JavaScript code for browser feature support. It should never inject third-party scripts, perform user redirection, fingerprint users, or evade detection through obfuscation and delayed execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate analytics or A/B testing scripts may inject scripts dynamically, but only from trusted, well-known domains and without obfuscation or evasion logic. They do not use typo-squatted domains or target users based on device and environment checks.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript payload served from cdn.polyfill.io
Dynamic script injection from typo-squatted domain (www.googie-anaiytics.com)
Selective targeting of mobile devices via user agent checks
Delayed execution using setTimeout to evade detection
Environment checks for admin or analytics presence to avoid analysis

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user visits a website that includes cdn.polyfill.io.
execution_context.file_location: Dynamically served JavaScript from cdn.polyfill.io, injected via <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v3/polyfill.min.js">.

package_info.package_manager: CDN (not a package manager, but a third-party JavaScript CDN service)
package_info.package_versions: All versions served after February 2024 (post-acquisition by Funnull)
package_info.why_malicious: After its acquisition by Funnull in February 2024, the polyfill.io CDN service began serving malicious, obfuscated JavaScript payloads. These payloads inject unwanted redirects, selectively target mobile users, evade detection through delayed execution and environment checks, and can potentially exfiltrate user data. The code is dynamically generated and adapts its behavior, turning every website that includes cdn.polyfill.io into a potential supply chain attack vector.

attack_chain.action: A website includes a script tag referencing cdn.polyfill.io, causing the browser to load and execute the malicious JavaScript payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes in the user's browser environment.

attack_chain.leads_to: Selective targeting of victims and evasion of security tools or manual analysis.

attack_chain.action: If targeting conditions are met, the code injects a script from a typo-squatted analytics domain or performs redirects to malicious sites.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is redirected to attacker-controlled content or further malicious payloads are loaded.

attack_chain.action: Potential for further attacks such as formjacking or data exfiltration if the payload evolves or is updated.
attack_chain.leads_to: Possible theft of user data, credentials, or sensitive information.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan website source code and network traffic for references to cdn.polyfill.io and typo-squatted analytics domains such as www.googie-anaiytics.com. Monitor for obfuscated JavaScript payloads that perform delayed execution, dynamic script injection, or conditional redirects. Use web application firewalls and browser security tools to block or alert on unexpected script sources and outbound requests to known malicious domains. Regularly audit third-party scripts and replace cdn.polyfill.io with trusted alternatives. Monitor for suspicious form data exfiltration to untrusted endpoints.
